Amaziah took courage, took his army, and went to the Valley of Salt, where he struck down ten thousand of the sons of Seir.
The sons of Judah captured another ten thousand and brought them to the top of the cavern. They hurled them down from the edge of the high plateau, and all of them perished.

The men of the army whom Amaziah had sent back, not allowing them to go with him to battle, raided the cities of Judah from Samaria to Beth-horon. They struck down three thousand of their inhabitants and took much plunder.
After Amaziah returned from striking down Edom, he brought to them the gods of the sons of Seir and set them up as his own gods. He bowed down before them and himself offered sacrifices to them.
The Lord’s anger came upon Amaziah, and he sent a prophet to him, who said to him, “Why have you sought the gods of that people, who did not save their own people from your hands?”

While he was speaking, Amaziah said to him, “Have they appointed you as the king’s adviser? Beware, lest you be tortured.” The prophet stopped speaking, but said, “I know that the Lord intends to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my advice.”
Amaziah took counsel and sent word to Joash son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, the king of Israel, saying, “Come, let us face one another.”

Joash king of Israel sent word to Amaziah king of Judah, saying, “The thornbush in Lebanon sent word to the cedar of Lebanon, saying, ‘Give your daughter to my son as his wife.’ But the wild animals of Lebanon’s wilderness passed by and trampled all the [?].”
“Look, you have struck down the Edomites, and your heart has made you proud of your glory. Stay at home from now on. Why should you fall into trouble and perish, you and Judah with you?”
But Amaziah did not listen, for it was the Lord’s doing to deliver him into the hands of Joash, because he had sought the gods of the Edomites.
Joash king of Israel went up, and he and Amaziah king of Judah faced one another at Beth-shemesh, which belongs to Judah.
Judah was defeated before Israel, and each man fled to his own home.

Joash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, son of Joash, at Beth-shemesh and brought him to Jerusalem. He tore down three hundred cubits of Jerusalem’s wall, from the Gate of Ephraim to the Corner Gate.
He took all the gold and silver and all the vessels found in the Lord’s house in the custody of Obed-edom, along with the treasures of the king’s house and the hostages, and returned to Samaria.
Amaziah son of Joash, king of Judah, lived for fifteen years after the death of Joash son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel.
As for the rest of Amaziah’s deeds, from first to last, are they not written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah?
When Amaziah turned away from the Lord, the troops in Jerusalem rose against him. He fled to Lachish, but they sent men after him to Lachish and killed him there.
They carried him on horses and buried him with his ancestors in the city of David.
All the people of the land took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah.
He rebuilt Elath and restored it to Judah after the king had died and joined his ancestors.
Uzziah was sixteen years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for fifty-two years. His mother’s name was Jecoliah, from Jerusalem.
He did what was right before the Lord, just as his father Amaziah had done.
He sought the Lord during the days of Zechariah, who was wise in the fear of the Lord. During his days Uzziah sought the Lord, and the Lord gave him success.
He went out and fought against the Philistines. He broke down the wall of Gath, the wall of Jabneh, and the wall of Ashdod, and built the cities of Ashdod among the Philistines.
The Lord strengthened him against the Philistines, against the Arabs who lived among the rocks, and against the Meunites.
The Meunites gave gifts to Uzziah, and his name became known as far as the entrance to Egypt, because he had become very powerful.
Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the Valley Gate and at the corners and fortified them.
He built towers in the wilderness and dug many wells, for he had many livestock in the Shephelah and on the plain, and vineyard workers in the hill country and in Carmel, because he loved farming.

Uzziah had troops who fought in war and went out to battle in divisions. Their numbers were recorded by Jeiel the chief scribe and Maaseiah the judge, under the direction of Hananiah, the king’s deputy.
The total number of heads of clans who were mighty in battle was two thousand six hundred.
Under them was a fighting force of three hundred seven thousand five hundred. They fought with great strength, helping the king against his enemies.
Uzziah prepared shields, spears, helmets, armor, bows, and slings for stones for the entire army.

In Jerusalem he made machines devised with skill to stand on the walls and at the corners, to shoot arrows and large stones. News of his preparations spread far away, for he was wonderfully helped until he became strong.
But when he became strong, his heart grew proud, leading to his ruin. He acted unfaithfully toward the Lord his God and entered the Lord’s temple to burn incense on the altar of incense.
Azariah the priest entered after him, accompanied by eighty courageous priests of the Lord.

They confronted King Uzziah and said to him, “It is not for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the Lord. It is for the priests, the descendants of Aaron who have been consecrated, to burn it. Leave the sanctuary, because you have rebelled against the Lord, and this will no longer bring you honor from the Lord God.”

Uzziah became angry, holding a censer in his hand to burn incense in the temple. As he grew angry with the priests, leprosy appeared on his forehead before the priests in the Lord’s house, at the altar of incense.
The chief priest and the other priests turned toward him, and there was leprosy on his forehead. They removed him from there, and he himself hurried to leave, because the Lord had rebuked him.

King Uzziah remained a leper until the day of his death. He lived as a leper in a separate house, because he had been excluded from the house of the Lord. His son Jotham was in charge of his kingdom, judging the people of the land.
The rest of Uzziah’s deeds, from first to last, were written by the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz.
Uzziah rested with his ancestors, and they buried him with his ancestors in the field of the kings’ burial ground, because they said, “He is a leper.” His son Jotham became king in his place.
Jotham was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for sixteen years. His mother’s name was Jerusha, daughter of Zadok.
He did what was right before the Lord, just as his father Uzziah had done in every respect, except that he did not enter the Lord’s temple. But the people were still corrupt.
He built the upper gate of the Lord’s house and built extensively on the wall of Ophel.
He built cities in the hill country of Judah, and settlements and towers in the forests.

He fought against the king of the Ammonites and prevailed over them. In one year the Ammonites gave him a hundred talents of silver, ten thousand kors of wheat, and ten thousand kors of barley. The king of Ammon brought this to him year by year, in the first year, the second, and the third.
Jotham grew strong because he set his ways in order before the Lord his God.
The rest of Jotham’s deeds, his war, and his battles are written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for sixteen years.
Jotham slept with his fathers and was buried in the City of David. His son Ahaz became king in his place.
Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for sixteen years. He did not do what was right before the Lord as his father David had done.
He followed the ways of the kings of Israel, for he made cast images,
and sacrificed to their idols in the land of Ben-hinnom. He made his sons pass through fire, following the abominations of the nations whom the Lord had destroyed before the Israelites.
He burned incense on the high places, on the rooftops, and under every leafy tree.

The Lord his God delivered him into the hands of the king of Syria, who defeated him, took many of his people captive, and brought them to Damascus. He also delivered him into the hands of the king of Israel, who inflicted great defeats on him.
Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, killed a hundred and twenty thousand mighty warriors in Judah in one day, because they had abandoned the Lord, the God of their fathers.
Zichri, a mighty warrior of Ephraim, killed Amaziah the king’s son, Azrikam the ruler of his household, and Elkanah, the king’s deputy.
The Israelites took captive three hundred thousand women, sons, and daughters from their brothers. They also took much plunder from them and brought the plunder to Samaria.

A prophet of the Lord named Oded was there. He went out to meet the army arriving in Samaria and said to them, “Look, the anger of the Lord, the God of your fathers, came upon Judah, and he delivered them into your hands. But you killed them in a rage that reached heaven.
And now you say that you will take the people of Judah and Jerusalem as your male and female slaves. Am I not here among you as a witness for the Lord your God?
Now listen to me and send back the captives whom you took from your brothers, for the Lord’s fierce anger is upon you.”
Then leaders of the Ephraimites—Azariah son of Johanan, Berechiah son of Meshillemoth, Hezekiah son of Shallum, and Amasa son of Hadlai—stood up against those returning from the war.

They said to them, “Do not bring these captives here to us, for you are making us sin against the Lord and adding to our sins and ignorant deeds. These sins of ours are already many, and the Lord’s fierce anger is upon Israel.”
So the warriors left the captives and the plunder before the leaders and the whole assembly.

All the men who had been called by name rose and cared for the captives. They clothed all those who were naked with clothing from the plunder, put shoes on their feet, gave them food, and anointed them with oil. They put all the weak on pack animals and brought them to their brothers at Jericho, the city of palm trees. Then they themselves returned to Samaria.
At that time Ahaz sent to the king of Assyria to help him,
because the Edomites had attacked Judah, struck it, and taken captives.

The Philistines advanced against the cities of the plain, and the Libyans came into Judah. They captured Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Soco and its villages, Timnah and its villages, and Gimzo and its villages, and settled there.
For the Lord humbled Judah because of Ahaz, king of Judah, because he had rebelliously turned away from the Lord.
Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, came against him and struck him.
Ahaz took what was in the house of the Lord, in the king’s house, and among the officials, and gave it to the king of Assyria, but there was no help for them.
Instead, he oppressed them, and Ahaz turned still further away from the Lord.

The king said, “I will seek the gods of Damascus, who struck me.” He said, “If the gods of the king of Assyria are the ones who give them strength, from now on I will sacrifice to them, and they will help me.” But they became a stumbling block to him and to all Israel.
Ahaz removed the vessels of the house of the Lord and broke them to pieces. He closed the doors of the house of the Lord and made himself an altar at every corner of Jerusalem.
In every city of Judah they made high places to burn incense to foreign gods, and they provoked the Lord, the God of their fathers, to anger.
The rest of his deeds, from first to last, are written in the book of the deeds of the kings of Judah and Israel.
Ahaz slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David, for they did not place him in the tombs of the kings. Hezekiah reigned in his place.
Hezekiah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Abijah, daughter of Zechariah.
He did what was right before the Lord, in accordance with everything that David his father had done.
When he began his reign, in the first month, he opened the doors of the house of the Lord and repaired them.
He brought in the priests and the Levites and stationed them on the eastern side.
He said to them, “Listen, Levites! Now sanctify yourselves and sanctify the house of the Lord, the God of your fathers, and remove the defilement from the holy places.
For our fathers rebelled and did evil before the Lord. They abandoned him, turned their faces away from the Lord’s tabernacle, and rebelled.
They closed the doors of the temple and extinguished the lamps. They did not burn incense to him or offer burnt offerings to the holy God of Israel.
The Lord became fiercely angry with Judah and Jerusalem and gave them over to folly, destruction, and hissing, as you see with your own eyes.
Our fathers have been wounded by swords, and your sons, your daughters, and your wives are in captivity in a land not their own, where they remain now.
From now on, let it be in our hearts to make a covenant with the Lord, the God of Israel, so that he may turn his fierce anger away from us.
Now do not fail to act from this time onward, for the Lord has chosen you to stand and serve before him, to be his ministers, and to burn incense.”

Then the Levites arose: Mahath son of Amasai and Joel son of Azariah, from the descendants of Kohath; Kish son of Abdi and Azariah son of Jehallelel, from the descendants of Merari; and Joah son of Zimmah and Joadan son of Joah, from the descendants of Gershon.
And from the descendants of Elizaphan, Shimri and Jeiel; and from the descendants of Asaph, Zechariah and Mattaniah;
and from the descendants of Heman, Jehiel and Shimei; and from the descendants of Jeduthun, Shemaiah and Uzziel.
They gathered their brothers and purified themselves, according to the king’s command and at the Lord’s command, to cleanse the house of the Lord.

The priests entered the house of the Lord to cleanse it. They brought out all the uncleanness found in the house of the Lord and in the courtyard of the house of the Lord, and the Levites took it away to the Kidron Valley.

They began to cleanse it on the first day, at the beginning of the first month. On the eighth day of the month they entered the Lord’s temple. They cleansed the house of the Lord over eight days and finished on the sixteenth day of the first month.

They went in to King Hezekiah and said, “We have cleansed everything in the house of the Lord: the altar of burnt offerings and its utensils, and the table for the bread of the Presence and its utensils.
And all the equipment that King Ahaz defiled during his reign and in his rebellion, we have prepared and purified. It is now before the altar of the Lord.”
King Hezekiah rose early, gathered the officials of the city, and went up to the Lord’s house.

He brought out seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats as a sin offering for the kingdom, for the sanctuary, and for Israel. He said to the sons of Aaron, the priests, “Offer them at the altar of the Lord.

And slaughter the bulls.” The priests received the blood and poured it against the altar. They slaughtered the rams and poured the blood against the altar, and they slaughtered the lambs and poured the blood against the altar.
They brought the male goats for the sin offering before the king and the people, and they laid their hands on them.

The priests slaughtered them and used their blood to make atonement at the altar. They made atonement for all Israel, because the king had said that the burnt offerings and the sin offerings were to be made for all Israel.

They stationed the Levites in the house of the Lord with cymbals, harps, and lyres, according to the command of King David, Gad the king’s seer, and Nathan the prophet, for this order was the Lord’s command through the prophets.
The Levites stood with David’s instruments, and the priests with the trumpets.

Hezekiah ordered the burnt offerings to be offered on the altar. When they began to offer the burnt offerings, they began to sing to the Lord with the trumpets and the instruments of David, king of Israel.
The whole assembly bowed down in worship, the psalm singers sang, and they sounded the trumpets until the burnt offerings were completed.
When they finished offering, the king and all the priests bowed down and worshiped.
King Hezekiah and the officials told the Levites to praise the Lord with the words of David and Asaph the prophet. They praised him joyfully, fell facedown, and worshiped.

Hezekiah responded and said, “Now consecrate yourselves to the Lord. From now on, come forward and bring offerings into the house of the Lord.” The assembly brought sacrifices of thanksgiving, and everyone whose heart was willing brought burnt offerings.
The number of burnt offerings that the assembly brought was seventy bulls, one hundred rams, and two hundred lambs. All these were burnt offerings to the Lord.
The consecrated offerings were six hundred bulls and three thousand sheep.

But the priests were few and could not slaughter all the burnt offerings. Their brothers, the Levites, helped them until the work was completed and until the priests had purified themselves, for the Levites purified themselves more willingly than the priests.

There were many burnt offerings, along with the fat of the consecration offerings, the peace offerings, and the offerings accompanying the burnt offerings. Thus the service in the house of the Lord was put in order.
Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced because the service of God had been prepared for the people, for this had happened suddenly.

Hezekiah sent word throughout all Israel and Judah and wrote a letter to Ephraim and Manasseh, telling them to come to the house of the Lord in Jerusalem and celebrate the Passover of the Lord, the God of Israel.
The king, the officials, and the whole assembly in Jerusalem decided to celebrate the Passover in the second month,
because they had been unable to celebrate it at its appointed time, since not enough priests had purified themselves and the people had not gathered in Jerusalem.
The proposal pleased the king and the assembly.

They resolved that heralds should travel throughout all Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, calling the people to come and celebrate the Passover of the Lord, the God of Israel, in Jerusalem, because the multitude had not observed it as prescribed in writing.

The couriers went throughout Israel and Judah with letters from the king and the officials, according to the king’s command. They said to the Israelites, “Return to the Lord, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and he will return to you who have survived and remain after escaping the hand of the king of Assyria.”
Do not be like your brothers and your fathers, who turned away from the Lord, the God of their fathers. He handed them over to destruction, as you yourselves see.
Now do not stiffen your necks. Give glory to God and enter his sanctuary, which he has consecrated forever. Serve the Lord your God, and he will turn his fierce anger away from you.

For when you return to the Lord, your brothers and your children will find compassion before all their captors, and he will bring them back to this land. For the Lord our God is merciful and compassionate, and he will not turn his face away from us if we return to him.
The messengers went from city to city in the hill country of Ephraim and Manasseh, as far as Zebulun, but people mocked and despised them.
But some men from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem.
In Judah also, the hand of the Lord was at work, giving them willing hearts to come and act according to the command of the king and the officials, in accordance with the word of the Lord.
Many people gathered in Jerusalem to celebrate the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the second month—a very large assembly.
They rose and tore down the altars that were in Jerusalem. They demolished all the places where incense was burned to false gods and threw them into the Kidron ravine.

They slaughtered the Passover sacrifice on the fourteenth day of the second month. The priests and the Levites were ashamed and purified themselves, and they brought the burnt offerings into the house of the Lord.
They stood at their stations according to their prescribed order, according to the command of Moses, the man of God, and the priests received the blood from the hands of the Levites.
For many in the assembly had not purified themselves, and the Levites slaughtered the Passover sacrifice for everyone who had been unable to become pure before the Lord.

For many of the people of Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun had not purified themselves, but ate the Passover contrary to what was written. Hezekiah prayed for them and said, “Good Lord, forgive all upright hearts.”
who seek you, the Lord, the God of their fathers, though they do not meet the requirements of purity for the holy things.
The Lord heard Hezekiah and healed the people.

The Israelites who were present in Jerusalem celebrated the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with great joy, praising the Lord day by day, while the priests and the Levites played instruments for the Lord.

Hezekiah spoke encouragingly to all the Levites and to the other wise men who had a good understanding of the service of the Lord. They observed the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days, slaughtering peace offerings and giving thanks to the Lord, the God of their fathers.
The assembly decided together to celebrate for another seven days, and they celebrated joyfully for seven more days.

For Hezekiah began giving the assembly of Judah a thousand young bulls and seven thousand sheep, and the leaders began giving the people a thousand young bulls and ten thousand sheep. A great many of the priests consecrated themselves.

The whole assembly rejoiced—the priests and Levites, all the people of Judah, those from Israel who were present there, the visitors who had come from the land of Israel, and the inhabitants of Judah.
There was great joy in Jerusalem, for since the days of Solomon son of David, king of Israel, there had not been such a festival in Jerusalem.
The Levitical priests rose and blessed the people. Their voice was heard, and their prayers reached the Lord’s holy dwelling in heaven.

When all this was finished, all the Israelites who were present went out to the cities of Judah. They smashed the pillars, cut down the groves, and demolished the high places and altars throughout Judah and Benjamin, and in Ephraim and Manasseh, until they had completely destroyed them. Then all Israel returned, each to his own inheritance and to their own cities.

Hezekiah appointed the priests and Levites to regular service, assigning each his daily duties according to his ministry, as priest or Levite: to offer burnt offerings and peace offerings, to bless and give thanks, and to serve at the gates of the courts of the Lord’s house.

The king’s contribution from his own possessions was for the morning and evening burnt offerings, and for the burnt offerings on Sabbaths, new moons, and the festivals prescribed in the law of the Lord.
He told the people living in Jerusalem to give the priests and Levites their portion, so that they could be strengthened in the service of the Lord’s house.
When the command was given, the Israelites brought still more firstfruits of grain, wine, oil, honey, and all the produce of the fields. They brought the tithes of everything in very great abundance.
The people of Israel and Judah who lived in the cities of Judah also brought tithes of cattle and sheep, and piled what they brought in heaps.
They began making the heaps in the third month and finished in the seventh month.
Hezekiah and the leaders came and saw the heaps, and they blessed the Lord and his people Israel.
Hezekiah questioned the priests and Levites about the heaps.

Azariah, the chief priest from the house of Zadok, said to him, “Since they began bringing these firstfruits into the Lord’s house, we have eaten and drunk and left these leftovers, because the Lord has blessed his people. This great abundance still remains.”
Hezekiah said, “Prepare additional storerooms in the Lord’s house.” And they prepared them.
They faithfully brought the firstfruits and tithes there. Conaniah the Levite was their overseer, and his brother Shimei was his deputy.

Jeiel, Uzziah, Nathan, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Semachiah, Mahath, Benaiah, and his sons who were there were under the authority of Conaniah and his brother Shimei, as King Hezekiah and Azariah, the leader of the Lord’s house, had commanded.
Kore son of Imnah, the Levite gatekeeper on the eastern side, was in charge of the roofs, to distribute the Lord’s firstfruits and the most holy things.

Through Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Mareshah, and Shecaniah, and through the priests, they faithfully distributed portions to their brothers according to their regular service, to the great and the small alike.
This was apart from the male descendants from the age of [?] upward, and everyone who entered the Lord’s house, counted day by day, for regular service according to their assigned order.

This was the enrollment of the priests according to their ancestral households, and of the Levites in daily service, from twenty years old and above, in their assigned order according to the register.
for all their offspring, their sons and daughters, together with the entire multitude, because they faithfully sanctified what was holy.

And for the sons of Aaron who were priests in their cities, there were designated men in every city who were appointed to give a portion to every male among the priests and to everyone enrolled among the Levites.
Hezekiah did this throughout Judah, and he did what was good and right before the Lord his God.
In every work he began to do in the house of the Lord, in accordance with the Lord’s laws and commandments, he sought his God. He acted with all his heart and prospered.
After these deeds and this faithfulness, Sennacherib king of Assyria came against Judah, encamped around the fortified cities, and declared that he would capture them.
Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had come against him to wage war against Jerusalem.
He consulted with the elders and the warriors about blocking the waters of the springs outside the city, and they blocked them.

He gathered a large multitude, and they blocked the waters of the springs and the river that divided as it passed through the middle of the city. They said, “The king of Assyria must not come and find abundant water and grow strong.”

Hezekiah strengthened himself and rebuilt all the demolished walls and the towers, and also the other wall outside the first wall. He strengthened the defenses of the City of David and prepared many weapons.
He appointed military commanders over the army, and they gathered around him in the square of the valley. He spoke to their hearts and said,
“Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid of the king of Assyria or of all the nations with him, because there are more with us than with him.
With him are arms of flesh, but with us is the Lord our God, to save us and fight our battles.” And the people were encouraged by the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.
After this, Sennacherib king of Assyria sent his servants to Jerusalem, while he himself was at Lachish with his entire army. He sent to Hezekiah king of Judah in Jerusalem and said,
“Thus says Sennacherib king of Assyria: What are you trusting in as you remain in the fortress of Jerusalem?
Is not Hezekiah deceiving you, handing you over to death by hunger and thirst, when he says, ‘The Lord our God will deliver us from the hands of the king of Assyria’?
Is this not the Hezekiah who demolished his altars and his high places and told Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, ‘Worship before this altar alone, and offer sacrifices on it’?
Do you not know what I and my fathers have done to all the peoples and regions? Were the gods of the nations of all the earth at all able to deliver their people from my hands?
Which of all the gods of those nations did my fathers not destroy? Were they able to save their people from my hands? And how will your God be able to deliver you from my hands?

Now do not let Hezekiah deceive you or give you hope in this. Do not believe him, because the gods of all the nations and kingdoms could not save their peoples from my hands or from the hands of my fathers. Your God will not deliver you from my hands.”
His servants said still more against the Lord God and against Hezekiah his servant.

He wrote a letter insulting the Lord, the God of Israel, and said concerning him, “Just as the gods of the nations of the earth did not deliver their peoples from my hands, so Hezekiah’s God will not save his people from my hands.”
He shouted loudly in Hebrew to the people of Jerusalem who were on the wall, to gain help for themselves and to tear down the wall, so that they could quickly capture the city.
And they spoke against the God of Jerusalem as they did against the gods of the peoples of the earth, which are the work of human hands.
King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz prayed about this and cried out to heaven.

And the Lord sent an angel and destroyed every mighty warrior, ruler, and commander in the camp of the king of Assyria. The king returned in shame to his own land and went into the house of his god, and those who had come from his own body struck him down there with the sword.
And the Lord saved Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem from the hand of Sennacherib king of Assyria and from the hand of everyone else, and gave them rest on every side.
And many brought offerings to the Lord in Jerusalem and gifts to Hezekiah king of Judah, and after this he was exalted in the eyes of all the nations.
In those days Hezekiah became sick and was near death. He prayed to the Lord, who heard him and gave him a sign.
But Hezekiah did not repay the kindness God had shown him. Instead, his heart became proud, and wrath came upon him and upon Judah and Jerusalem.
And Hezekiah humbled himself from the pride of his heart, as did the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and the Lord’s wrath did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah.
Hezekiah had very great wealth and glory, and he made himself treasuries for gold, silver, precious stones, incense, weapons, and valuable vessels.
And he made towns for storing grain, wine, and oil, and villages and quarters for all the livestock, and pens for the flocks.
And the cities that he built for himself, and large stocks of sheep and cattle, because the Lord gave him very great possessions.
Hezekiah himself [?] the upper outlet of the waters of Gihon and directed the water downward to the western side of the City of David. And Hezekiah prospered in all his works.

And this is how he acted toward the messengers of the rulers who were sent to him from Babylon to inquire about him and the signs that had occurred in the land. And the Lord left him to test him and to know what was in his heart.
And the rest of Hezekiah’s deeds and his acts of mercy are written in the prophecy of the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz and in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.

And Hezekiah rested with his fathers, and they buried him on the height where the tombs of the descendants of David were. All Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem gave him glory and honor at his death, and his son Manasseh reigned in his place.
Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned in Jerusalem for fifty-five years.
And he did evil before the Lord, following all the abominations of the nations whom the Lord had destroyed before the Israelites.
And he rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had demolished, erected images of the Baals, made groves, and bowed down to all the host of heaven and served them.
And he built an altar in the house of the Lord, of which the Lord had said, “My name shall be in Jerusalem forever.”
There he built altars for all the hosts of heaven in both courtyards of the house of the Lord.

And he made his sons pass through fire in the land of Ben-hinnom, practiced divination, sought omens from birds, practiced sorcery, and appointed mediums and enchanters. He greatly increased his evil deeds before the Lord, provoking him to anger.

And the carved and cast image which he made in the house of the Lord, about which God said to David and to his son Solomon, “In this house and in Jerusalem, which I chose from all the tribes of Israel, I will place my name forever.”

And I will no longer drive Israel from this land that I gave to their ancestors, provided that they take care to do everything I commanded them, according to all the laws, statutes, and ordinances given through Moses.
And Manasseh led Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem astray, making them do more evil than all the nations that the Lord had removed before the Israelites.
And the Lord spoke to Manasseh and his people, but they did not listen.
And the Lord brought against him the commanders of the army of the king of Assyria. They captured him, bound him with chains, and took him to Babylon.
And when he was in distress, he sought the favor of the Lord his God and humbled himself greatly before the God of his ancestors.
He prayed to him, and God heard his cry and brought him back to Jerusalem, to his kingdom. And Manasseh knew that the Lord was God.

And after this he built a wall outside the city of David, on the west along the southern side in the ravine, and toward the exits of the gates, all around Ophel. He made it very high and stationed army commanders in all the fortified cities of Judah.
And he removed the foreign gods and the carved images from the house of the Lord, and all the altars that he had built on the mountain of the house of the Lord, in Jerusalem, and outside the city.
And he restored the altar of the Lord and offered sacrifices of deliverance and praise upon it. And he told Judah to serve the Lord, the God of Israel.
But the people still went to the high places; nevertheless, the Lord was their God.
And the rest of the deeds of Manasseh, his prayer to God, and the words of the seers who spoke to him in the name of the Lord, the God of Israel—

behold, they are in the accounts of his prayers and of how he was heard. And all his sins and his rebellion, and the places where he built high places and set up sacred groves and carved images before his conversion—behold, they are written in the accounts of the seers.
And Manasseh rested with his ancestors, and they buried him in the garden of his house. And his son Amon reigned in his place.
Amon was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned for two years in Jerusalem.
And he did evil before the Lord, as his father Manasseh had done. Amon sacrificed to all the idols that his father Manasseh had made and served them.
And he did not humble himself before the Lord as his father Manasseh had humbled himself, but his son Amon multiplied his sins.
And his servants rose up against him and killed him in his own house.
And the people of the land struck down those who had risen against the king, and the people of the land made his son Josiah king in his place.
Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned for thirty-one years in Jerusalem.
And he did what was right before the Lord and walked in the ways of his ancestor David. He did not turn aside to the right or to the left.

And in the eighth year of his reign, while he was still a boy, he began to seek the Lord, the God of his ancestor David. And in the twelfth year of his reign he began to cleanse Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, the sacred groves, and the cast images.

And he demolished the altars of the Baals in his presence, along with the raised places on which they stood. He broke apart the sacred groves, smashed and ground up the carved and cast images, and scattered them before the tombs of those who had sacrificed to them.
And he burned the bones of the priests on the altars and cleansed Judah and Jerusalem,
and the cities of Ephraim and Manasseh, of Simeon and Naphtali, and their surrounding places.
He removed the sacred groves and the altars, crushed the idols into small pieces, and removed all the high places from the land of Israel. Then he returned to Jerusalem.

In the eighteenth year of his reign, when he had finished purifying the land and the royal house, he sent Shaphan son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Josiah son of Joahaz, the recorder of his records, to repair the house of the Lord his God.

They came to Hilkiah the high priest, and he handed over the silver that had been brought into the house of the Lord. The Levites who guarded the entrance had collected it from Manasseh and Ephraim, from the leaders and all the remnant of Israel, and from the people of Judah and Benjamin and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
They gave it into the hands of those responsible for the work, who were in the house of the Lord to restore and repair the house.
They gave it to the carpenters and builders to buy large squared stones and timber for beams, to roof the buildings that the kings of Judah had torn down.

These men carried out the work faithfully. Their overseers were Jahath and Obadiah, Levites descended from Merari, and Zechariah and Meshullam, descended from Kohath, who supervised them, along with every Levite skilled in musical instruments.
They were in charge of the burden-bearers and those who did the work and prepared for the work. Among the Levites were chief scribes, judges, and gatekeepers.
As they were taking out the silver that had been brought into the house of the Lord, Hilkiah the priest found the book of the law of the Lord given through Moses.
Hilkiah spoke to Shaphan the chief scribe and said, “I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord.” Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan.
Shaphan brought the book to the king and gave the king an account of all the silver handed over to his servants who were doing the work.
They melted down the silver found in the house of the Lord and gave it into the hands of the overseers and those who were doing the work.
Shaphan the chief scribe told the king, “Hilkiah the priest gave me a book of the law.” Then Shaphan read it before the king.
When the king heard the words of the law, he tore his robe.
The king gave orders to Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Obadiah son of Micaiah, Shaphan the chief scribe, and Asaiah the king’s servant, saying:

“Go and inquire of the Lord for me and for all those remaining in Israel and Judah concerning the words of this book that has been found. For great is the Lord’s wrath that has been kindled against us, because our fathers did not obey the words of the Lord by doing everything written in this book.”

Hilkiah and those to whom the king had spoken went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum son of Tokhath, son of Hasrah, who kept the commandments. She lived in Jerusalem, in Masena. They spoke to her about these matters.
She said to them, “This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: Tell the man who sent you to me:
‘This is what the Lord says: I am bringing disaster upon this place—all the words written in the book that was read before the king of Judah—
because they abandoned me and sacrificed to foreign gods, provoking me to anger with the works of their hands. My wrath has been kindled against this place and will not be extinguished.’
But to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the Lord, say this: ‘This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says concerning the words you heard:

And your heart was reverent, and you humbled yourself before me when you heard my words against this place and its inhabitants. You humbled yourself before me, tore your robes, and wept before me, and I have heard you, says the Lord.

Behold, I will gather you to your ancestors, and you will be laid in your grave in peace. Your eyes will not see all the disasters that I will bring upon this place and its inhabitants. And they brought these words back to the king.
And the king sent word and gathered the elders of Judah and Jerusalem.

And the king of Judah went up to the house of the Lord, together with all Judah, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the priests, the Levites, and all the people, from the greatest to the least. He read in their hearing all the words of the covenant that had been found in the house of the Lord.

And the king rose and stood on the pillar. He made a covenant before the Lord to follow the Lord and, with all his heart and all his soul, to keep his commandments, his testimonies, his decrees, and the words of the covenant written in that book.
And he made everyone who was in Jerusalem and Benjamin take their stand, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem made a covenant in the house of the God of their ancestors.

And Josiah removed all the abominations from all the land belonging to the Israelites, and he made everyone who was in Jerusalem and Israel serve the Lord their God. Throughout his life he did not turn away from following the Lord, the God of his ancestors.
And Josiah celebrated the Passover to the Lord his God, and they slaughtered the Passover sacrifices on the fourteenth day of the first month.
And he assigned the priests to their duties and encouraged them in the work of the house of the Lord.

And he told the Levites and the mighty men throughout Israel to consecrate themselves to the Lord. They placed the holy ark in the house that Solomon, son of David, king of Israel, had built. And the king said, “You have nothing to carry on your shoulders. Now serve the Lord your God and his people Israel.”
“And prepare yourselves according to your ancestral households and the rotations of your service, as written by David, king of Israel, and by his son King Solomon.”

“And stand in the temple according to the divisions of your ancestral households, before your brothers and the members of your people, and according to the division of the household of your tribe, the Levites.”
“And slaughter the Passover sacrifices and prepare the holy things for your brothers, to act according to the word of the Lord given through Moses.”

And Josiah began giving the people rams, ewes, and young male goats, all for the Passover, for everyone who was present: thirty thousand animals in all, and three thousand bulls. These came from the king’s possessions.

And his officials began giving to the people, the priests, and the Levites. Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, officials of the house of God, gave the priests two thousand six hundred rams, ewes, and male goats for the Passover, and three hundred bulls.

And Conaniah and his brothers Benaiah, Shemaiah, and Nethanel, together with Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad, leaders of the Levites, began giving the Levites five thousand rams and five hundred bulls for the Passover.
And the service was arranged, and the priests stood in their assigned order and the Levites in their divisions, according to the king’s command.
And they slaughtered the Passover sacrifices, and the priests poured out the blood from their hands, while the Levites skinned the animals.

And they prepared the burnt offerings to give them to each person according to the divisions of the ancestral houses of the people, to offer them to the Lord, as it is written in the book of the law of Moses. Likewise in the mornings.
And they roasted the Passover offerings over the fire according to the law, and boiled the sacred offerings in pots and kettles. This went well, and they hurried to all the people.

And afterward they prepared for themselves and for the priests, because the priests were offering the fat and the burnt offerings until night. So the Levites prepared for themselves and for their brothers, the sons of Aaron.

And the singers of psalms, the sons of Asaph, were at their stations according to the command of David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, the king’s prophets. The leaders and the gatekeepers were at each gate, and they could not leave their sacred service, because their brothers, the Levites, prepared for them.
And all the service of the Lord was put in order and prepared that day, to celebrate the Passover and offer the burnt offerings on the altar of the Lord, according to the command of King Josiah.
And the Israelites who were present there celebrated the Passover at that time and the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days.

And no Passover like it had ever been celebrated in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet. None of the kings of Israel had celebrated a Passover like the one celebrated by Josiah, the priests, the Levites, all Judah and Israel who were present there, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

They celebrated it for the Lord in the eighteenth year of Josiah’s reign. And King Josiah removed and burned with fire the mediums, diviners, soothsayers, idols, and sorcerers who were in the land of Judah and in Jerusalem, so that he might establish the words of the law written in the book that Hilkiah the priest found in the house of the Lord. Before him there was no one like him who turned to the Lord God with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his strength, according to all the law of Moses; and after him no one like him arose. Nevertheless, the Lord did not turn from his great, furious anger, with which the Lord was enraged against Judah because of all the provocations with which Manasseh had angered him. And the Lord said, “I will also reject Judah from my presence, as I rejected Israel, and I will cast away the city that I chose, Jerusalem, and the house of which I said, ‘My name shall be there.’”
And Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, went up against the king of Assyria at the Euphrates River, and King Josiah went out against him.

And he sent messengers to him and said, “What have I to do with you, king of Judah? I have not come against you today to wage war, and God told me to hurry. Beware of God, who is with me, lest he destroy you.”

And Josiah did not turn away from him, but strengthened himself to fight against him. He did not listen to the words of Neco, which came from the mouth of the Lord, and he came to fight in the plain of Megiddo.
And the archers struck King Josiah, and the king said to his servants, “Take me away from here, for I am badly wounded.”
And his servants took him out of his chariot and put him in his second chariot, and brought him to Jerusalem. He died and was buried with his fathers, and all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah.

And Jeremiah uttered laments for Josiah, and all the leaders, men and women, uttered laments for Josiah to this day. They established this as an ordinance in Israel, and behold, they are written in the book of laments.
And the acts of Josiah and his hope were written in the law of the Lord.
And the rest of his acts, from first to last, behold, are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.
The people of the land took Jehoahaz son of Josiah, anointed him, and made him king in Jerusalem in place of his father.

Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for three months. His mother’s name was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah, from Libnah. He did evil in the sight of the Lord, just as his ancestors had done.

Pharaoh Neco bound him at Riblah in the land of Hamath, so that he would no longer reign in Jerusalem. The king took him to Egypt and imposed a tribute of one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold on the land.

Pharaoh Neco made Eliakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, king in place of his father Josiah, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. Pharaoh Neco took his brother Jehoahaz and brought him to Egypt, where he died. They gave the silver and gold to Pharaoh. From that time onward, the land began to pay tribute, and they gave the silver as Pharaoh commanded. They demanded silver and gold from the people of the land, from each person according to his means, to give it to Pharaoh Neco.

Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother’s name was Zechora, daughter of Neriah, from Ramah. He did evil in the sight of the Lord, just as his ancestors had done. In his days Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up into the land, and he served him for three months, then rebelled against him. The Lord sent the Chaldeans and the raiding bands of the Syrians, the Moabites, the Ammonites, and Samaria. After these events they withdrew, according to the word of the Lord through his servants the prophets. Nevertheless, wrath from the Lord was upon Judah, to remove it from his presence because of the sins of Manasseh, in everything he had done, and because of the innocent blood that Manasseh had shed, filling Jerusalem with innocent blood. Yet the Lord did not wish to destroy them.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against him, bound him with bronze fetters, and took him to Babylon.
He also took some of the vessels of the Lord’s house to Babylon and placed them in his temple in Babylon.

The rest of the deeds of Jehoiakim and everything he did—are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? Jehoiakim rested with his ancestors and was buried with his ancestors in the Garden of Uzza. His son Jeconiah became king in his place.
Jeconiah was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for three months and ten days. He did evil in the sight of the Lord.

At the turn of the year, King Nebuchadnezzar sent for him and took him to Babylon, along with the precious vessels of the Lord’s house. He made Zedekiah, his father’s brother, king over Judah in Jerusalem.
Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eleven years.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord his God. He showed no respect for Jeremiah the prophet or for the words of the Lord.

When he rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar and broke the oaths that the king had made him swear by his God, he stiffened his neck and hardened his heart, refusing to return to the Lord, the God of Israel.
All the leading men of Judah, the priests, and the people of the land committed more and more lawless acts, following the abominations of the nations, and defiled the Lord’s house in Jerusalem.
The Lord, the God of their ancestors, sent to them through the prophets. He sent his messengers early, because he had compassion on his people and on his sanctuary.
They despised his messengers, scorned his words, and mocked the prophets, until the Lord’s anger rose against his people, and there was no longer any remedy for them.

And he brought against them the king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in his sanctuary. He did not spare Zedekiah or show mercy to their young women, and he handed over all their old men into their hands.
And he took to Babylon all the utensils of the house of God, large and small, and all the treasure of the king and his nobles—everything.
And he burned the house of the Lord, demolished the wall of Jerusalem, burned its palaces with fire, and destroyed every beautiful vessel.
And he took the survivors captive to Babylon, and there they served him and his sons until the reign of the Medes.
This fulfilled the word of the Lord spoken through Jeremiah, until the land received its Sabbaths. It kept Sabbath rest throughout all the days of its desolation, until seventy years were completed.

In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, after the word of the Lord spoken through Jeremiah had been fulfilled, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, and he ordered a proclamation to be made in writing throughout his whole kingdom, saying:

Thus says Cyrus, king of Persia: The Lord, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has commanded me to build him a house in Jerusalem in Judea. Whoever among you is one of his people, may the Lord his God be with him, and let him go up.
